items.stem: Which Japanese prime minister was shot by an ultranationalist in November 1930, partly in anger at his acceptance of the London Naval Treaty?
items.answer: Hamaguchi Osachi
items.markingKey: Hamaguchi Osachi. Hamaguchi was shot at Tokyo Station in November 1930 and died in 1931; Inukai was assassinated in May 1932.

items.stem: Hana writes: "The Depression did not affect Japan because its economy was not linked to the USA." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Japan depended heavily on silk exports to the USA, and the collapse of US demand after 1929 caused severe rural distress that strengthened militarist and expansionist arguments.
items.markingKey: Japan depended heavily on silk exports to the USA, and the collapse of US demand after 1929 caused severe rural distress that strengthened militarist and expansionist arguments. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between the Kōdōha and the Tōseiha.
items.answer: The Kōdōha (Imperial Way) was a radical faction of young officers seeking a violent “Shōwa Restoration” and war with the USSR; the Tōseiha (Control Faction) favoured disciplined, bureaucratic mobilisation of the economy for total war, working through the existing state. After the failed 1936 coup the Tōseiha dominated.
items.markingKey: The Kōdōha (Imperial Way) was a radical faction of young officers seeking a violent “Shōwa Restoration” and war with the USSR; the Tōseiha (Control Faction) favoured disciplined, bureaucratic mobilisation of the economy for total war, working through the existing state. After the failed 1936 coup the Tōseiha dominated. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Source A
There are only three ways left to Japan to escape from the pressure of surplus population. The first door, emigration, has been barred to us by the anti-Japanese immigration policies of other countries. The second door, the advance into world markets, is being pushed shut by tariff barriers. When two of the three doors have been closed, it is quite natural that Japan should rush upon the last remaining door – the expansion of territory.
— Hashimoto Kingorō, army officer and founder of the ultranationalist Cherry Blossom Society, in “Addresses to Young Men”, late 1930s (adapted)

What is the message of Source A about the causes of Japanese expansion in the early 1930s? [2]
items.answer: Japan faced overpopulation; emigration was blocked by foreign anti-Japanese immigration laws; tariffs shut Japan out of world markets; so territorial expansion was presented as the only remaining and natural option.
items.markingKey: Japan faced overpopulation; emigration was blocked by foreign anti-Japanese immigration laws; tariffs shut Japan out of world markets; so territorial expansion was presented as the only remaining and natural option. Award 1 mark for each valid point about the message, up to [2]; a description of the source without interpretation of its message scores at most 1.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the 26 February Incident (1936) shows the growth of military influence over government.
items.answer: About 1,400 troops led by Kōdōha officers seized central Tokyo and killed former prime minister Saitō Makoto and finance minister Takahashi Korekiyo before the coup was suppressed on the emperor’s orders. Although the coup failed, the Tōseiha used it to purge rivals and increase the army’s say over the cabinet; the military budget rose sharply after Takahashi’s death.
items.markingKey: Context (About 1,400 troops led by Kōdōha officers seized central Tokyo and killed former prime minister Saitō Makoto and finance minister Takahashi Korekiyo before the coup was suppressed on the emperor’s orders.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "The weakness of civilian government was a greater cause of Japanese expansion than the strength of nationalism."
items.answer: The two were interdependent: nationalism supplied the motive and popular backing, while institutional weakness meant civilians could not restrain the military.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: constitutional independence of the military (right of supreme command); assassinations of Hamaguchi (1930) and Inukai (1932); cabinets accepted faits accomplis in Manchuria. Arguments against: popular nationalism and press enthusiasm for the Manchurian venture; ideology of kokutai shared by officers and many civilians; nationalism explains why weak governments could not resist. Supported judgement: The two were interdependent: nationalism supplied the motive and popular backing, while institutional weakness meant civilians could not restrain the military.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "gekokujō"?
options: The puppet state created by Japan in Manchuria in 1932, nominally headed by the last Qing emperor, Puyi
The clash between Japanese and Chinese troops near Beijing on 7 July 1937 that escalated into full-scale war between Japan and China
The freezing of Japanese assets and the halt of US oil exports to Japan in July–August 1941, after Japan occupied southern Indochina
Literally “the low overturning the high”: insubordination by junior officers who took action without orders and presented their superiors with a fait accompli
items.answer: Literally “the low overturning the high”: insubordination by junior officers who took action without orders and presented their superiors with a fait accompli
items.markingKey: D. "gekokujō" is literally “the low overturning the high”: insubordination by junior officers who took action without orders and presented their superiors with a fait accompli.

items.stem: Distinguish between ideological motives for Japanese expansion and economic motives for Japanese expansion.
items.answer: Economic motives concerned raw materials, markets and land in response to the Depression and population pressure; ideological motives concerned kokutai, a sense of Japan’s mission to lead Asia (pan-Asianism) and rejection of Western liberal values.
items.markingKey: Economic motives concerned raw materials, markets and land in response to the Depression and population pressure; ideological motives concerned kokutai, a sense of Japan’s mission to lead Asia (pan-Asianism) and rejection of Western liberal values. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Source C
Just as a proletarian within a nation has the right to fight against unjust inequality, so Japan, a proletarian nation among nations, has the right to make war on those countries that monopolise vast territories. The Constitution should be suspended, the Diet dissolved and martial law declared so that the people and the emperor together can carry out the reconstruction of the nation.
— Kita Ikki, radical nationalist thinker, “An Outline Plan for the Reorganisation of Japan”, written 1919 and published 1923 (paraphrased)

With reference to the origin, purpose and content of Source C, assess its values and limitations for historians investigating the causes of Japanese expansion in the early 1930s. [4]
items.answer: Value: It shows the ideological roots of the radical young officers, many of whom read Kita; it illustrates the link between domestic revolution and expansion. Limitations: It is a theoretical programme written a decade before 1931 by one individual; it does not show government policy, and Kita was executed after the 1936 coup, which suggests the state rejected his methods.

items.stem: Explain why Japan signed the Tripartite Pact in 1940.
items.answer: Germany’s victories in 1940 left French and Dutch colonies in Southeast Asia vulnerable; Japan hoped the pact would deter the USA from intervening as Japan moved south (northern Indochina, September 1940) and would secure German recognition of its New Order.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the Marco Polo Bridge Incident escalated into full-scale war in 1937.
items.answer: After the Xi’an Incident (1936) Chiang Kai-shek had agreed to a united front with the CCP and was under pressure not to concede more; the Konoe government sent reinforcements expecting a quick victory, and fighting spread to Shanghai in August 1937.

items.stem: Briefly describe the Nanjing Massacre (December 1937–January 1938) and explain what it reveals about the brutality of Japanese expansion and its effect on international opinion.
items.answer: Japanese troops killed large numbers of prisoners and civilians and committed mass rape after the fall of Nanjing; estimates range from tens of thousands to over 300,000 dead. Reports by Western residents (e.g. John Rabe) shocked opinion abroad, hardening US and British hostility to Japan and stiffening Chinese resistance.

items.stem: Explain why the US oil embargo of 1941 pushed Japan towards war.
items.answer: Japan imported around 80 per cent of its oil from the USA; without oil its navy and army would be paralysed within about two years, so leaders felt they must either withdraw from China (unacceptable) or seize the oil of the Dutch East Indies, which required neutralising the US fleet.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the Panay incident (12 December 1937) shows the limits of the US response to Japanese aggression in the late 1930s.
items.answer: Japanese aircraft sank the US gunboat Panay on the Yangtze near Nanjing, killing three people; Japan apologised and paid compensation. Despite outrage the USA accepted an apology because isolationism and the Neutrality Acts made war politically impossible, showing that Washington was not yet ready to confront Japan.

items.stem: Using the Brussels Conference (November 1937) as an example, explain the collapse of collective security in East Asia by 1937.
items.answer: The signatories of the Nine-Power Treaty met to address the Sino-Japanese war; Japan refused to attend and the conference ended without action. Even after full-scale war and atrocities, the powers could agree only on a mild statement, showing that the framework of treaties and the League no longer restrained Japan.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "Tripartite Pact".
items.answer: The alliance signed in Berlin on 27 September 1940 by Germany, Italy and Japan, pledging mutual assistance if any were attacked by a power not yet at war
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the alliance signed in Berlin on 27 September 1940 by Germany, Italy and Japan, pledging mutual assistance if any were attacked by a power not yet at war. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the international response to Japanese expansion in 1940–41 and the international response to Manchuria (1931–33).
items.answer: In 1931–33 the response was limited to investigation and moral condemnation (Lytton Report, Stimson Doctrine) with no sanctions; in 1940–41 the USA, Britain and the Netherlands used economic weapons – embargoes and asset freezes – that directly threatened Japan’s ability to fight.
items.markingKey: In 1931–33 the response was limited to investigation and moral condemnation (Lytton Report, Stimson Doctrine) with no sanctions; in 1940–41 the USA, Britain and the Netherlands used economic weapons – embargoes and asset freezes – that directly threatened Japan’s ability to fight. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Japan left the League because it had been expelled for invading Manchuria." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Japan was not expelled; it chose to leave after the Assembly adopted the Lytton Report against it.
items.markingKey: Japan was not expelled; it chose to leave after the Assembly adopted the Lytton Report against it. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "The Depression did not affect Japan because its economy was not linked to the USA." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Japan depended heavily on silk exports to the USA, and the collapse of US demand after 1929 caused severe rural distress that strengthened militarist and expansionist arguments.
items.markingKey: Japan depended heavily on silk exports to the USA, and the collapse of US demand after 1929 caused severe rural distress that strengthened militarist and expansionist arguments. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "The Second Sino-Japanese War ended quickly with the fall of Nanjing in 1937." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Chiang moved the capital to Wuhan and then Chongqing and kept fighting; the war became a stalemate and lasted until 1945.
items.markingKey: Chiang moved the capital to Wuhan and then Chongqing and kept fighting; the war became a stalemate and lasted until 1945. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why the League of Nations failed to take effective action over Manchuria.
items.answer: The League had no army; Britain and France, the leading members, were preoccupied with the Depression and unwilling to risk war or trade in the Far East; the USA and USSR were not members; the Lytton commission took a year to report, by which time Manchukuo was a fact.

(2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Source C
If the League could not act effectively in Manchuria, where the facts were clear, it could hardly hope to deter any great power in future. After 1933 many governments drew the conclusion that their security lay in armaments and alliances rather than in Geneva.
— Ruth Henig, British historian, in The League of Nations (2010) (paraphrased)

What, according to Source C, were the main features of the collapse of collective security in East Asia? [3]
items.answer: Manchuria was a clear test that the League failed; its failure undermined deterrence of great powers; states turned to rearmament and alliances.

items.stem: Hana writes: "The civilian government in Tokyo planned each stage of Japanese expansion from 1931." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Much expansion was initiated by the Kwantung Army acting without authorisation (gekokujō), as at Mukden in 1931; civilian cabinets often accepted faits accomplis rather than directing policy.
items.markingKey: Much expansion was initiated by the Kwantung Army acting without authorisation (gekokujō), as at Mukden in 1931; civilian cabinets often accepted faits accomplis rather than directing policy. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to the Nanjing Massacre (December 1937–January 1938), explain how it illustrates the brutality of Japanese expansion and its effect on international opinion.
items.answer: Japanese troops killed large numbers of prisoners and civilians and committed mass rape after the fall of Nanjing; estimates range from tens of thousands to over 300,000 dead. Reports by Western residents (e.g. John Rabe) shocked opinion abroad, hardening US and British hostility to Japan and stiffening Chinese resistance.

items.stem:
Source B
Japan has been forced into a position in which she must either accept the encirclement of the ABCD powers and the slow strangulation of her national life, or break through by force. If we do nothing, our oil will be exhausted within two years and the navy will become a useless ornament.
— Remarks attributed to Navy Chief of Staff Nagano Osami at the Imperial Conference, 6 September 1941, as recorded in the conference minutes (paraphrased)

What is the message conveyed by Source B? [2]
items.answer: Japan felt encircled by America, Britain, China and the Dutch; the oil embargo meant reserves would be exhausted in about two years; the choice was between slow strangulation and war.

items.stem: With reference to the Brussels Conference (November 1937), explain how it illustrates the collapse of collective security in East Asia by 1937.
items.answer: The signatories of the Nine-Power Treaty met to address the Sino-Japanese war; Japan refused to attend and the conference ended without action. Even after full-scale war and atrocities, the powers could agree only on a mild statement, showing that the framework of treaties and the League no longer restrained Japan.

items.stem:
Source A
There are only three ways left to Japan to escape from the pressure of surplus population. The first door, emigration, has been barred to us by the anti-Japanese immigration policies of other countries. The second door, the advance into world markets, is being pushed shut by tariff barriers. When two of the three doors have been closed, it is quite natural that Japan should rush upon the last remaining door – the expansion of territory.
— Hashimoto Kingorō, army officer and founder of the ultranationalist Cherry Blossom Society, in “Addresses to Young Men”, late 1930s (adapted)

With reference to the origin, purpose and content of Source A, assess its values and limitations for historians investigating the causes of Japanese expansion in the early 1930s. [4]
items.answer: Value: It shows how a leading radical officer justified expansion to a domestic audience and reveals the economic and demographic arguments used by ultranationalists. Limitations: As propaganda written to win support for expansion, it presents expansion as unavoidable and blames foreign powers, ignoring alternatives and the role of the military’s own ambitions; it was written with hindsight after Manchuria.

items.stem:
Source D
The Japanese troops acted in self-defence against Chinese soldiers who had blown up the railway. The Imperial Army has no territorial ambitions in Manchuria; it seeks only to protect Japanese lives and treaty rights against the lawlessness of Chinese warlords.
— Statement issued by the Japanese government to the League of Nations, September 1931 (paraphrased)

With reference to the origin, purpose and content of Source D, assess its values and limitations for historians investigating Japanese expansion in China between 1931 and 1940. [4]
items.answer: Value: It is the official Japanese justification at the start of the crisis and shows how Japan sought to present its actions as legal to the League. Limitations: Its purpose was to deflect international criticism; the claim of Chinese sabotage was false (the explosion was staged by Kwantung officers), and the occupation of all Manchuria and creation of Manchukuo contradicted it.

items.stem: A student claims that the attack on Pearl Harbor was an unprovoked act unrelated to US policy. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It followed the US oil embargo and asset freeze of July–August 1941 and the Hull Note of November 1941, which Japanese leaders saw as leaving them a choice between retreat from China and war.

items.stem: Explain the difference between appeasement and collective security.
items.answer: Collective security meant states acting together through the League to deter or punish aggression; appeasement meant individual states making concessions to an aggressor to avoid war. The failure of the first in the 1930s encouraged reliance on the second.
items.markingKey: Collective security meant states acting together through the League to deter or punish aggression; appeasement meant individual states making concessions to an aggressor to avoid war. items.stem: Explain the difference between the Kōdōha and the Tōseiha.
items.answer: The Kōdōha (Imperial Way) was a radical faction of young officers seeking a violent “Shōwa Restoration” and war with the USSR; the Tōseiha (Control Faction) favoured disciplined, bureaucratic mobilisation of the economy for total war, working through the existing state. After the failed 1936 coup the Tōseiha dominated.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the occupation of Manchuria (1931–32) and the Second Sino-Japanese War from 1937.
items.answer: Manchuria was a limited, regional operation initiated by the Kwantung Army that ended with the Tanggu Truce (1933); from 1937 Japan fought an all-out, open-ended war against the Nationalist government and the CCP across China, with mass civilian casualties and no clear end.

items.stem: Using the 26 February Incident (1936) as an example, explain the growth of military influence over government.
items.answer: About 1,400 troops led by Kōdōha officers seized central Tokyo and killed former prime minister Saitō Makoto and finance minister Takahashi Korekiyo before the coup was suppressed on the emperor’s orders. Although the coup failed, the Tōseiha used it to purge rivals and increase the army’s say over the cabinet; the military budget rose sharply after Takahashi’s death.

items.stem: With reference to the battle of Shanghai (August–November 1937), explain how it illustrates the escalation of the conflict into a war of attrition.
items.answer: Chiang committed elite German-trained divisions; around 200,000 Chinese and tens of thousands of Japanese troops became casualties before Japan took the city. It showed that China would resist rather than negotiate and that Japan’s hope of a swift victory was unrealistic, leading to a prolonged war that drained Japanese resources.

items.stem: "The weakness of civilian government was a greater cause of Japanese expansion than the strength of nationalism." With reference to specific examples, discuss. [15]
items.answer: The two were interdependent: nationalism supplied the motive and popular backing, while institutional weakness meant civilians could not restrain the military.
items.markingKey: Paper 2 essay.
